pudendal nerve: Arises from S2–S4, passes through the sciatic foramina into Alcock's canal; supplies the perineal muscles, external sphincters and skin of the external genitalia. It is blocked during childbirth.
putamen: Outer part of the lentiform nucleus; with the caudate it forms the striatum and is the commonest site of hypertensive haemorrhage.
pyramid of medulla oblongata: Anterior swelling formed by the corticospinal fibres; about 85% of them cross at its lower end (pyramidal decussation).
pyramis of vermis: Pyramid-shaped lobule of the inferior vermis.
radial nerve: Continuation of the posterior cord; runs in the spiral groove of the humerus and supplies all the extensors. A humeral shaft fracture or 'Saturday night palsy' causes wrist drop.
red nucleus: Iron-containing nucleus in the midbrain tegmentum; the origin of the rubrospinal tract, it receives cerebellar output.
retina: Inner layer containing the visual cells; the fovea at the centre of the macula is the site of sharpest vision.
roots of brachial plexus: Anterior rami of C5–T1; they emerge between the scalene muscles.
rubrospinal tract: Descending pathway from the red nucleus that increases flexor muscle tone.
saphenous nerve: Longest sensory branch of the femoral nerve; passes through the adductor canal and supplies the inner side of the leg and foot. It can be injured when the saphenous vein is harvested.
sciatic nerve: Thickest nerve in the body, formed from L4–S3; emerges below piriformis into the gluteal region and divides in the back of the thigh into the tibial and common fibular nerves.
sclera: White, tough outer layer of the eyeball; it gives attachment to the eye muscles.
sensory root of trigeminal nerve: Large root running from the trigeminal ganglion to the pons.
septal nuclei: Limbic nuclei below the septum pellucidum; they take part in the reward and pleasure circuit.
septum pellucidum: Thin membrane separating the anterior horns of the two lateral ventricles.
spinal dura: Tough membrane surrounding the spinal cord; it ends at S2 and is separated from the vertebral canal by the epidural space (epidural anaesthesia).
spinal ganglion: Ganglion on the dorsal root containing the cell bodies of sensory neurons; the herpes zoster virus lies latent here.
spinal reticular process: Network beside the dorsal horn where grey and white matter mix.
spinotectal tract: Carries sensory information to the superior colliculus, orienting the head and eyes.
straight gyrus (gyrus rectus): Gyrus on the inferior surface of the frontal lobe at the midline, medial to the olfactory sulcus.
stria medullaris thalami: Fibre bundle running along the upper medial border of the thalamus to the habenula.
stria terminalis: Fibre pathway from the amygdala to the hypothalamus along the edge of the caudate nucleus.
subclavian nerve: Arises from the upper trunk and supplies subclavius.
subparietal sulcus: Sulcus on the medial surface separating the precuneus from the cingulate gyrus.
sulcus interm_prim-jensen: Small sulcus separating the supramarginal and angular gyri.
superficial branch of radial nerve: Sensory branch to the lateral back of the hand; it can be compressed by a tight watch strap (Wartenberg).
superficial branch of ulnar nerve: Carries palmar sensation from the medial one and a half fingers and supplies palmaris brevis.
superficial fibular nerve: Supplies the lateral compartment muscles and most of the skin of the dorsum of the foot.
superior cerebellar peduncle: Main output pathway of the cerebellum; carries fibres from the dentate nucleus to the thalamus and red nucleus.
superior colliculus: Visual reflex centre; it turns the eyes and head towards visual stimuli.
superior frontal gyrus: Upper gyrus of the frontal lobe; its medial part contains the supplementary motor area.
superior frontal sulcus: Separates the superior and middle frontal gyri.
superior gluteal nerve: Emerges above piriformis; supplies gluteus medius and minimus and TFL. Its injury causes a Trendelenburg gait.
superior lateral brachial cutaneous nerv: Superior lateral cutaneous nerve of arm
Carries sensation from the skin over deltoid (the 'badge' area).
superior occipital gyri: Upper gyrus of the lateral surface of the occipital lobe.
superior parietal lobule: Lobule above the intraparietal sulcus; linked to body schema and spatial perception.
superior salivatory nucleus: Nucleus of the parasympathetic fibres (VII) to the lacrimal, submandibular and sublingual glands.
superior subscapular nerve: Supplies the upper part of subscapularis.
superior temporal gyrus (lateral part): Its posterior part contains Wernicke's area (Brodmann 22); damage on the dominant side causes fluent (sensory) aphasia.
superior temporal sulcus: Separates the superior and middle temporal gyri.
superior trunk of brachial plexus: Formed by the union of the C5–C6 roots; its stretching at birth causes Erb–Duchenne palsy ('waiter's tip').
supramarginal gyrus: Gyrus capping the posterior end of the lateral fissure (Brodmann 40); on the dominant side it takes part in language processing.
suprascapular nerve: Arises from the upper trunk, passes through the scapular notch and supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus.
sural nerve: Carries sensation from the posterolateral leg and the lateral border of the foot; used for nerve biopsy and grafts.
suspensory ligament of eyeball: Hammock-like thickening of fascia supporting the eyeball from below.
sympathetic nerves: Branches from the sympathetic trunk to the organs and vessels; they include the splanchnic nerves.
sympathetic trunk: Chain of ganglia on either side of the vertebral column from the skull base to the coccyx; damage to the cervical ganglia causes Horner syndrome.
tectospinal tract: From the superior colliculus to the neck muscles; a reflex pathway turning the head towards visual stimuli.
tegmentum of pons: Dorsal part of the pons containing cranial nerve nuclei, sensory pathways and the reticular formation.
temporal plane: Flat area behind Heschl's gyrus; larger in the dominant hemisphere and involved in language processing.
temporal pole: Anterior tip of the temporal lobe.
tentorium cerebelli: Tent of dura separating the cerebellum from the occipital lobes; the brainstem passes through its notch, and uncal herniation occurs at this edge.
thalamus: Large mass of grey matter forming the side walls of the third ventricle; the relay station to the cortex for all senses except smell.
third ventricle: Narrow cavity between the two thalami; connected to the lateral ventricles by the foramina of Monro and to the fourth ventricle by the aqueduct of Sylvius.
thoracodorsal nerve: Arises from the posterior cord and supplies latissimus dorsi; preserved for the flap in breast reconstruction.
tibial nerve: Medial branch of the sciatic nerve; descends from the popliteal fossa into the calf, supplies the posterior compartment muscles and passes through the tarsal tunnel to the sole.
tonsil of cerebellum: Rounded lobule beside the inferior vermis; with raised intracranial pressure it can herniate through the foramen magnum and compress the medulla (displaced downwards in Chiari malformation).
transverse frontopolar gyrus and sulcus*: Transverse gyri and sulci at the frontal pole.
transverse occipital sulcus: Continuation of the intraparietal sulcus in the occipital lobe.
transverse temporal gyri: Primary auditory cortex (Brodmann 41, 42) on the surface of the superior temporal gyrus inside the lateral fissure.
triangular part of inferior frontal gyru: Triangular part of inferior frontal gyrus
trigeminal nerve (v): Largest cranial nerve; carries sensation from the face (V1, V2, V3) and supplies the muscles of mastication (V3). Trigeminal neuralgia most often affects the V2–V3 territory.
trochlear nerve (iv): Supplies superior oblique; the only and thinnest cranial nerve leaving the back of the brainstem, with the longest intracranial course.
tuber of vermis: Lobule in the posterior inferior vermis.
tympanic membrane: Thin membrane separating the external and middle ear; the umbo and cone of light are seen on otoscopy, and paracentesis is done in the posteroinferior quadrant.
ulnar nerve: Arises from the medial cord and passes behind the medial epicondyle (the 'funny bone'); supplies most intrinsic hand muscles and sensation of the medial one and a half fingers. Injury causes a claw hand.
uvula of vermis: Lobule of the inferior vermis between the two tonsils.
vagus nerve (x): Cranial nerve with the widest distribution, carrying parasympathetic fibres to the neck, chest and abdominal organs and motor fibres to the pharynx and larynx; the efferent limb of the gag reflex.
vestibular nerve: Part carrying balance information from the semicircular canals, utricle and saccule; its inflammation is vestibular neuritis.
vestibular nuclei: Four nuclei receiving balance information; they regulate eye movements and posture through the vestibulospinal tracts and the MLF.
vestibule: Middle part of the inner ear; with the utricle and saccule it senses linear acceleration.
vestibulocochlear nerve (viii): Carries hearing and balance; a vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) at the cerebellopontine angle causes one-sided hearing loss.
vitreous body: Transparent gel filling the space between the lens and the retina.
white matter of spinal cord: Anterior, lateral and posterior funiculi containing the ascending and descending tracts.
white matter of telencephalon: Myelinated fibres beneath the cortex: association, commissural and projection fibres.
wing of central lobule: Wings of the central lobule extending into the hemisphere.
zonular fibres: Fibres suspending the lens from the ciliary body; they weaken in Marfan syndrome, causing lens dislocation.
